title: Ramyeon Ttukbaegi
subtitle: Pot-cooked instant noodles with egg and kimchi
excerpt: A single portion of instant noodles is cooked directly in a Korean earthenware pot with kimchi, garlic, gochugaru and an egg cracked in at the end. The earthenware retains heat so the noodles stay hot in the pot at the table and the egg cooks gently from the residual steam. This serves 1 and takes 15 minutes. It is deliberately simple and very good.
sourceNotes: Ramyeon has been eaten in Korea since the 1960s when instant noodles were introduced as an affordable food source. Cooking it in a ttukbaegi rather than a regular pot is the home-cook's method that keeps the noodles hot at the table and gives the dish a slightly different character from restaurant preparation. Adding kimchi, eggs and extra seasoning to elevate instant noodles is considered an art form in Korea.

glossaryTerms.definition: A ttukbaegi is a Korean earthenware pot, dark brown or grey in colour, used for cooking and serving dishes directly at the table. It retains heat far longer than metal pans, which is why food served in a ttukbaegi arrives still bubbling and continues to cook slightly from the residual heat at the table. Ttukbaegi are used for doenjang jjigae, sundubu jjigae, and ramyeon among many other dishes. They are available in Korean supermarkets and online.

Ramyeon is the Korean term for instant noodles, distinct from Japanese ramen in flavour profile, heat level and seasoning packet contents. Korean ramyeon is typically spicier, uses a gochugaru-based broth powder, and is designed to be cooked in the pot it is served in. Popular brands include Shin Ramyun, Neoguri and Buldak. Each brand has its own flavour packet and recommended water amount, so follow the packet instructions as a base.

content.text: This recipe serves 1 and takes 15 minutes. The dish is built around the
: the earthenware pot you cook, serve and eat from without transferring the noodles.
cooked this way stays hot for the full time it takes to eat it, and the pot develops a slight crust at the bottom that many people consider the best part.

If you do not have a ttukbaegi, a small heavy saucepan works fine, but the dish loses its characteristic table-side bubbling. The kimchi should be fermented, not fresh, so that it has developed sourness. Very fresh kimchi tastes raw here. Older, more sour kimchi is better.
Place the ttukbaegi on the hob over a medium heat. Add the water specified on the ramyeon packet, the garlic, gochugaru if using, and the kimchi. Bring to the boil.

Add the seasoning packet from the ramyeon and stir to dissolve. Add the noodles and tofu if using. Cook according to the packet instructions, usually 4 to 5 minutes, keeping the broth at a steady simmer.
When the noodles are almost cooked, crack the egg directly into the centre of the pot. Do not stir. Let it sit for 1 to 2 minutes until the white is just set but the yolk is still soft.
Add the spring onions and a few drops of sesame oil. Carry the ttukbaegi carefully to the table using a cloth or oven gloves, as it will be very hot. Serve directly from the pot.

items.symptom: Noodles have turned to mush by the time they reach the table
items.cause: The noodles were cooked for too long before serving
items.fix: Ramyeon noodles continue cooking in the residual heat of the ttukbaegi. Pull them off the heat 30 seconds before they reach your desired texture.

items.cause: The full seasoning packet was used with too little water
items.fix: Use the water amount specified on the packet exactly. If it still tastes too salty after cooking, add a small splash of extra water and stir. Adding more kimchi or tofu can also dilute and balance the seasoning.

items.symptom: Egg white is still raw but yolk has set
items.cause: The egg was cracked in too late, or the broth was not hot enough when the egg was added
items.fix: Crack the egg in with about 2 minutes of cooking time remaining, not at the last moment. The broth should be at a gentle simmer when the egg goes in. A lid placed over the pot for 1 minute helps the white set faster.

content.text: Ramyeon in a ttukbaegi is a late-night dish, a solo meal, a comfort food eaten after a long day with little energy to cook. It appears in Korean dramas and films because it signals something: the character is tired, hungry and making do. In reality, it is not making do at all. Korean instant noodles are delicious, and upgrading them with kimchi, a good egg and the right pot turns them into something worth making by choice, not just necessity.
